Content:
In this lesson, we will discuss how to maximize or minimize the sum, product, difference, and quotient of two numbers taken from closed intervals. This will be very useful for some of the work that follows.

Content:
Watch Out! We'll only consider closed intervals of numbers in this lesson. Recall that closed intervals are defined using "or equal to" compound inequalities, such as
[MATH: 1\leq x \leq 5]
or, using interval notation,
[MATH: x\in [1,5].]

Content:
The rules we'll discuss here do not apply to open or semi-open intervals, such as
[MATH: 3< y < 5\qquad\text{or}\qquad 8 < x \leq 12.]

Content:
Also, it will be necessary to restrict our attention to positive numbers when discussing products and quotients.

Content:
Suppose we have two numbers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] such that

Content:
[MATH: 1\leq a \leq 7\qquad\text{and}\qquad 4\leq b \leq 8.]

Content:
What is the largest possible value of [MATH: a + b?]

Content:
We can answer this question by applying the following principle:

Content:
> To maximize the sum of two numbers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b,] we must add the largest possible value of [MATH: a] to the largest possible value of [MATH: b.]

Content:
So, let's compute the largest possible values of [MATH: a] and [MATH: b,] and find their sum:

Content:
- Since [MATH: 1\leq a \leq 7,] the largest possible value of [MATH: a] is [MATH: 7.] We'll write this as follows:
[MATH: \max(a) = 7]
- Since [MATH: 4\leq b \leq 8,] the largest possible value of [MATH: b] is [MATH: 8.]
[MATH: \max(b) = 8]

Content:
Therefore,
[MATH: max(a + b)|= max(a) + max(b); = 7 + 8; = 15.]

Content:
The rule for maximizing a product is similar, though it only works for positive numbers:

Content:
> To maximize the product of two positive numbers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b,] we must multiply the largest possible value of [MATH: a] by the largest possible value of [MATH: b.]

Content:
So, in this example, we have
[MATH: max(ab)|= max(a) ⋅ max(b); = 7 ⋅ 8; = 56.]

Content:
Note: We can think of [MATH: \max(a)] as a function that takes a number [MATH: a] as input and returns the largest possible value of [MATH: a] as output, and similarly for [MATH: \max(b).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To minimize the product of two positive numbers [MATH: p] and [MATH: q,] we must multiply the smallest possible value of [MATH: p] by the smallest possible value of [MATH: q.]

More precisely, if [MATH: a, b, c,] and [MATH: d] are positive numbers such that [MATH: a\leq p\leq b\quad\textrm{and}\quad c\leq q\leq d] then the minimum value of [MATH: pq] equals [MATH: min(pq)|= min(p) ⋅ min(q); = ac.]

In this case, [MATH: \min(p) = 1] and [MATH: \min(q) = 6.] Therefore, [MATH: min(p) ⋅ min(q) = 1 ⋅ 6 = 6.]

Take a moment to appreciate why this must be true. If we're trying to maximize a difference, we want to start with the largest number possible and then subtract as little as possible from it.

So, let's compute the largest possible value of [MATH: a,] the smallest possible value of [MATH: b,] and find their difference:

- Since [MATH: 4\leq b \leq 8,] the smallest possible value of [MATH: b] is [MATH: 4.]
[MATH: \min(b) = 4]

Content:
Therefore,
[MATH: max(a − b)|= max(a) − min(b); = 12 − 4; = 8.]

Content:
The rule for maximizing a quotient is similar, though it only works for positive numbers:

Content:
> To maximize the quotient of two positive numbers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b,] we take the largest possible value of [MATH: a] and divide by the smallest possible value of [MATH: b.]

Content:
Again, take a moment to appreciate why this must be true. We want the dividend to be as large as possible, while the divisor should be as small as possible.

Content:
So, in this example, we have
[MATH: max((a)/(b))|= (max(a))/(min(b)); = (12)/(4); = 3.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we will discuss how to maximize or minimize the sum, product, difference, and quotient of two numbers taken from closed intervals. This will be very useful for some of the work that follows.

Content:
Watch Out! We'll only consider closed intervals of numbers in this lesson. Recall that closed intervals are defined using "or equal to" compound inequalities, such as
[MATH: 1\leq x \leq 5]
or, using interval notation,
[MATH: x\in [1,5].]

Content:
The rules we'll discuss here do not apply to open or semi-open intervals, such as
[MATH: 3< y < 5\qquad\text{or}\qquad 8 < x \leq 12.]

Content:
Also, it will be necessary to restrict our attention to positive numbers when discussing products and quotients.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Maximizing a Sum or Product

Content:
Suppose we have two numbers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] such that

Content:
[MATH: 1\leq a \leq 7\qquad\text{and}\qquad 4\leq b \leq 8.]

Content:
What is the largest possible value of [MATH: a + b?]

Content:
We can answer this question by applying the following principle:

Content:
> To maximize the sum of two numbers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b,] we must add the largest possible value of [MATH: a] to the largest possible value of [MATH: b.]

Content:
So, let's compute the largest possible values of [MATH: a] and [MATH: b,] and find their sum:

Content:
- Since [MATH: 1\leq a \leq 7,] the largest possible value of [MATH: a] is [MATH: 7.] We'll write this as follows:
[MATH: \max(a) = 7]
- Since [MATH: 4\leq b \leq 8,] the largest possible value of [MATH: b] is [MATH: 8.]
[MATH: \max(b) = 8]

Content:
Therefore,
[MATH: max(a + b)|= max(a) + max(b); = 7 + 8; = 15.]

Content:
The rule for maximizing a product is similar, though it only works for positive numbers:

Content:
> To maximize the product of two positive numbers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b,] we must multiply the largest possible value of [MATH: a] by the largest possible value of [MATH: b.]

Content:
So, in this example, we have
[MATH: max(ab)|= max(a) ⋅ max(b); = 7 ⋅ 8; = 56.]

Content:
Note: We can think of [MATH: \max(a)] as a function that takes a number [MATH: a] as input and returns the largest possible value of [MATH: a] as output, and similarly for [MATH: \max(b).]

---

Item 3 — Tutorial: Minimizing a Sum or Product

Content:
Let's consider our two intervals once more:

Content:
[MATH: 1\leq a \leq 7\qquad\text{and}\qquad 4\leq b \leq 8.]

Content:
What is the smallest possible value of [MATH: a + b?]

Content:
We can answer this question by applying the following principle:

Content:
> To minimize the sum of two numbers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b,] we must add the smallest possible value of [MATH: a] to the smallest possible value of [MATH: b.]

Content:
So, let's compute the smallest possible values of [MATH: a] and [MATH: b,] and find their sum:

Content:
- Since [MATH: 1\leq a \leq 7,] the smallest possible value of [MATH: a] is [MATH: 1.] We'll write this as follows:
[MATH: \min(a) = 1]
- Since [MATH: 4\leq b \leq 8,] the smallest possible value of [MATH: b] is [MATH: 4.]
[MATH: \min(b) = 4]

Content:
Therefore,
[MATH: min(a + b)|= min(a) + min(b); = 1 + 4; = 5.]

Content:
The rule for minimizing a product is similar, though it only works for positive numbers:

Content:
> To minimize the product of two positive numbers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b,] we must multiply the smallest possible value of [MATH: a] by the smallest possible value of [MATH: b.]

Content:
So, in this example, we have
[MATH: min(ab)|= min(a) ⋅ min(b); = 1 ⋅ 4; = 4.]

---

Item 4 — Example: Optimizing Sums and Products

More precisely, if [MATH: a, b, c,] and [MATH: d] are positive numbers such that
[MATH: a\leq p\leq b\quad\textrm{and}\quad c\leq q\leq d]
then the minimum value of [MATH: pq] equals
[MATH: min(pq)|= min(p) ⋅ min(q); = ac.]

In this case, [MATH: \min(p) = 1] and [MATH: \min(q) = 6.] Therefore,
[MATH: min(p) ⋅ min(q) = 1 ⋅ 6 = 6.]
